title: Transition Elements
tagline: Variable oxidation states, colour, catalysis and complexes — the d-block in action.

overview.intro: Transition elements are defined by an incomplete d sub-shell in the atom or a common ion, and everything distinctive about them follows from those d electrons. They show several oxidation states because the 4s and 3d energies are close, they are coloured because d–d transitions absorb visible light, they catalyse reactions because they offer variable states and surface sites, and they form complexes with defined geometries and isomerism. The chapter treats iron, copper, manganese and chromium as the working examples, since these are the ones the syllabus and the papers name.

facts.label: Definition
facts.value: Element with an incomplete d sub-shell in the atom or in a common oxidation state.

facts.label: Variable states
facts.value: Mn shows +2 to +7, Fe +2 and +3, Cu +1 and +2, from 4s/3d proximity.

facts.label: Complexes
facts.value: Central metal ion surrounded by ligands; coordination numbers 4 and 6 are common.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Colour, catalysis, complex formation and alloy questions recur every year.

learningOutcomes: Define transition elements and distinguish them from zinc and other d-block elements.
Explain variable oxidation state, colour, catalytic activity and magnetic behaviour with examples.
Describe the preparation, structure and reactions of potassium manganate(VII) and potassium dichromate(VI).
Explain complex formation, coordination number, ligand types and geometrical isomerism.
Account for the formation and properties of alloys and interstitial compounds.

learn.title: Characteristic properties of the transition elements

blocks.text: The d-block elements occupy groups 3 to 12, but only those with an incomplete d sub-shell in the atom or in a common ion are true transition elements — which is why zinc, cadmium and mercury, with a filled d sub-shell in every common state, are excluded despite sitting in the block. Because the (n−1)d and ns orbitals are close in energy, electrons can be removed from both, giving several oxidation states that vary across the period: manganese reaches +7 in manganate, iron shows +2 and +3, copper +1 and +2. The d electrons also give colour, because absorbing a photon promotes an electron between split d levels and the complementary colour is transmitted, and they give magnetism, since unpaired d electrons produce a magnetic moment. Metallically they are hard, dense, high-melting and form alloys, and they catalyse reactions by offering variable oxidation states and by adsorbing reactants on their surface.

items: Variable oxidation state: the 4s and 3d electrons are close enough in energy to be lost in different numbers.
Colour arises from d–d transitions; Zn2+ and Sc3+ are colourless because their d sub-shells are full or empty.
Catalysis: Fe in the Haber process, V2O5 in the contact process, Ni in hydrogenation, MnO2 in peroxide decomposition.
Interstitial compounds such as steel trap small atoms of hydrogen, carbon or nitrogen in the lattice, making the metal harder.
Alloys form because atoms of similar size substitute for one another, as in brass, an alloy of copper and zinc.
Complex ions form because the metal ion has vacant orbitals to accept lone pairs from ligands.
Melting points and enthalpies of atomisation are high across the middle of the series, pepping near manganese and then falling.

items.note: The surface adsorbs nitrogen and hydrogen, weakening their bonds and lowering the activation energy.

items.text: Copper(II) sulphate solution is blue while zinc sulphate is colourless
items.note: Cu2+ has an incomplete d sub-shell able to absorb visible light; Zn2+ with d^10 cannot.

blocks.caption: Why transition elements behave as they do

blocks.text: Two oxidants carry the analytical chemistry of this course. Potassium manganate(VII) is prepared by fusing manganese dioxide with potassium hydroxide in the presence of air, giving the green manganate, which is then oxidised electrolytically to the deep purple permanganate. In acidic solution it is reduced to colourless Mn2+, accepting five electrons, which makes it a self-indicating titrant: the first permanent pink marks the endpoint. Potassium dichromate(Vi) is prepared by fusing chromite ore with sodium carbonate and then treating with acid, giving orange crystals. It accepts three electrons on reduction to the green Cr3+ ion. Both oxidise in different ways — permanganate oxidises iodide to iodine and iron(II) to iron(III), while dichromate oxidises hydrogen sulphide to sulphur and sulphur dioxide to sulphate — and both change colour on reduction, which is why they are used as indicators and in redox titrations.

items: Preparation of KMnO4: 2MnO2 + 4KOH + O2 → 2K2MnO4 + 2H2O, then electrolytic oxidation of manganate.
Acidified permanganate half-reaction: MnO4− + 8H+ + 5e− → Mn2+ + 4H2O, purple to colourless.
Dichromate half-reaction: Cr2O7^2− + 14H+ + 6e− → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O, orange to green.
In neutral or faintly alkaline solution permanganate is reduced only to MnO2, a brown precipitate.
Both oxidants bleach by oxidation, unlike sulphur dioxide which bleaches by reduction.
Dichromate is preferred when an acid that permanganate would attack is present.

items.note: The purple colour discharges as peroxide is oxidised to oxygen, used to standardise the solution.
Orange turns green as Cr(VI) becomes Cr3+, the basis of the breathalyser reaction.

items.meaning: Species that accepts electrons and is itself reduced.
Titrant whose own colour change marks the endpoint without an added indicator.
FeCr2O4, the raw material for dichromate manufacture.
Simultaneous oxidation and reduction of one species, as manganate to manganate and permanganate in acid.

blocks.text: A complex consists of a central metal ion or atom surrounded by ligands, which are molecules or ions that donate a lone pair to form coordinate bonds. The number of ligands bonded is the coordination number, most commonly 4 or 6: four ligands usually give a tetrahedral or square planar geometry and six an octahedron. Ligands are classified by how many pairs they donate — monodentate such as water, ammonia and cyanide, bidentate such as ethylenediamine, and hexadentate EDTA which wraps around a single metal ion. Isomerism arises in two main ways. Geometrical isomers differ in the relative positions of ligands: cis and trans in a square planar complex or cis and trans in an octahedral one. Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions. Naming follows a fixed order: ligands alphabetically first with their count prefixes, then the metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals.

items: Ligand donation requires a lone pair, so Lewis bases act as ligands and the metal ion is the Lewis acid.
Coordination number 4 → tetrahedral or square planar; coordination number 6 → octahedral.
Chelation, the attachment of a multidentate ligand such as EDTA, stabilises the complex greatly.
Cis–trans isomerism needs two different ligands in a plane or on opposite positions of an octahedron.
Optical isomerism requires a non-superimposable mirror image, which is why cis-bis(ethylenediamine) complexes rotate plane-polarised light.
The coordination sphere is written in square brackets: [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 has six ammonia ligands inside and chloride outside.

items.note: The two chlorides adjacent give the cis form used in chemotherapy; opposite gives trans.
Six cyanide ligands, then iron with its +2 oxidation state named as an anion.

learn.title: Iron, copper and manganese in practice

blocks.text: The syllabus names three d-block elements for detailed study, and each shows the general properties in its own way. Iron exists as +2 and +3; the +2 state is a mild reducing agent that is oxidised in air, while the +3 state is the stable form in neutral solution and gives the yellow colour of iron(III) solutions. The test for iron(III) with ammonium hydroxide gives a reddish-brown precipitate, and with thiocyanate a blood-red colour, while iron(II) gives a dirty green precipitate. Copper shows +1 and +2, with copper(I) disproportionating in aqueous solution to copper metal and copper(II) because the hydrated +2 ion is the more stable. Manganese is the showcase: the purple permanganate, the green manganate, the brown dioxide and the nearly colourless +2 ion, each reachable by choosing the conditions. Extraction of copper by electrolysis of copper sulphate with an impure anode and a pure cathode is the industrial application to learn.

items: Iron(III) + NH4OH → reddish-brown Fe(OH)3; iron(II) gives dirty green Fe(OH)2, darkening in air.
Fe3+ + SCN− gives the blood-red [Fe(SCN)]2+ complex, the standard test for iron(III).
2Cu+ → Cu + Cu2+ in water: copper(I) disproportionates because Cu2+ is stabilised by hydration.
Electrolytic refining: impure copper anode dissolves and pure copper deposits on the cathode.
Manganese’s common states: +2 nearly colourless, +3 purple, +4 brown, +6 green, +7 purple.
Steel is iron with up to 1.5% carbon, with other metals added for specific properties.

items.text: Adding sodium hydroxide to iron(III) chloride
items.note: A reddish-brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide confirms the +3 ion.

items.text: Copper anode in an electrolytic refinery
items.note: The anode loses mass while the cathode gains pure copper, and anode sludge holds the precious metals.

keyPoints: Transition elements have an incomplete d sub-shell in the atom or a common ion.
Zinc, cadmium and mercury are d-block but not transition elements.
Variable oxidation state arises from the close energies of ns and (n−1)d orbitals.
Colour comes from d–d transitions; ions with full or empty d sub-shells are colourless.
Transition metals catalyse by variable oxidation states and by surface adsorption.
Acidified permanganate is reduced from purple MnO4− to colourless Mn2+ accepting five electrons.
Dichromate goes from orange to green on reduction to Cr3+.
Complexes comprise a metal centre with ligands; coordination numbers 4 and 6 give defined geometries.
Geometrical isomers differ by position; optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images.
Alloys and interstitial compounds explain the hardness and utility of transition metals.
examFocus: Define transition elements with the d sub-shell condition and immediately exclude zinc as the discriminator.
Colour questions need the absorption plus complementary colour, not the phrase d–d transition alone.
Redox titration answers should state the change in oxidation number for both the permanganate and the analyte.
Complex naming: ligands alphabetically, then metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals.

vocabulary.meaning: Element with an incomplete d sub-shell in the atom or a common oxidation state.
Molecule or ion donating a lone pair to a central metal atom.
Number of ligand donor atoms bonded to the central metal ion.
Ring structure formed when a multidentate ligand binds a metal at two or more points.
Promotion of an electron between split d orbitals by absorbed visible light.
Compound with small atoms trapped in the holes of a metal lattice.
Mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, altering its properties.
Substance that accepts electrons and oxidises another species.
Isomerism from a difference in the spatial arrangement of ligands.
Attraction to a magnetic field caused by unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: Which element is a d-block element but not a transition element?
questions.explanation: Zinc has a completely filled d sub-shell, d^10, in the atom and in Zn2+, so it fails the definition.

questions.prompt: The colour of a transition-metal complex is due to:
options: d–d transitions of electrons between split d orbitals
questions.answer: d–d transitions of electrons between split d orbitals
questions.explanation: Absorbing visible light promotes an electron across the ligand-field splitting energy, and the complementary colour is transmitted.

questions.prompt: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) is reduced to:
questions.explanation: In acidic solution permanganate accepts five electrons per manganese, giving nearly colourless Mn2+ ions.

questions.prompt: The complex [Co(NH3)2Cl4] shows which type of isomerism?
questions.explanation: Two ammonia ligands may sit adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans) in the octahedron, giving geometrical isomers.

questions.prompt: The number of ligand donor atoms attached to the central metal ion in a complex is called its coordination __________ .
questions.explanation: Coordination number 4 commonly gives tetrahedral or square planar geometry and 6 gives an octahedron.

questions.prompt: The substance that accepts electrons and is itself reduced during a reaction is called an __________ agent.
questions.explanation: An oxidising agent oxidises the other species while being reduced itself.

questions.prompt: Why are compounds of Sc3+ and Zn2+ colourless while those of Cu2+ are coloured?
questions.answer: Sc3+ has no d electrons, d^0, and Zn2+ has a completely filled sub-shell, d^10, so neither can promote an electron between split d levels. Cu2+ has nine d electrons, so a d–d transition is possible in the visible range and the complementary colour is transmitted.
questions.explanation: Colour requires both an empty-to-full set of options: a partially filled d sub-shell is essential.

questions.prompt: Give two ways in which transition elements act as catalysts and name one example of each.
questions.answer: First, they offer variable oxidation states and alternate between them during the reaction, as iron cycles between Fe2+ and Fe3+ in the Haber process. Second, they adsorb reactants on their surface and weaken the bonds, as nickel adsorbs hydrogen in the hydrogenation of oils.
questions.explanation: Homogeneous catalysis follows the redox route, heterogeneous catalysis the surface route.

questions.prompt: Describe the laboratory preparation of potassium manganate(VII) and its reactions with hydrogen peroxide and with iron(II) sulphate in acidic solution.
questions.answer: Manganese dioxide is fused with potassium hydroxide in the presence of air, giving green potassium manganate; oxidation of the manganate, electrolytically or with chlorine, then gives the deep purple potassium manganate(VII). With hydrogen peroxide in acid the permanganate is reduced to Mn2+ while peroxide is oxidised to oxygen, discharging the purple colour. With iron(II) sulphate in acid, permanganate oxidises Fe2+ to Fe3+ and is itself reduced to Mn2+, accepting one electron per iron and five per manganese; the titration is self-indicating because the first permanent pink marks the endpoint.
questions.explanation: The five-electron reduction of permanganate sets every stoichiometric ratio in these titrations.

questions.prompt: Explain why copper(I) compounds are unstable in aqueous solution while copper(II) compounds are stable, and write the disproportionation equation.
questions.answer: In water the small Cu+ ion is strongly hydrated, and the hydration energy released is insufficient to compensate for the sum of the ionisation energies needed to reach Cu+. Cu2+ gains much more hydration energy because of its higher charge, so the +2 state is stabilised by water. Consequently copper(I) disproportionates: 2Cu+(aq) → Cu(s) + Cu2+(aq), in which one ion is reduced to metal and the other oxidised to +2. Copper(I) compounds survive only in insoluble or complexed forms such as CuCl and [Cu(CN)2]−.
questions.explanation: Competition between ionisation energy and hydration energy decides the stable oxidation state in water.
